front.title: Optional IS-IS Packet Timestamping and Database Fingerprint

abstract.t: Many applications in today’s networks rely on reliable and timely flooding of link-state information, such as, but not limited to Traffic Engineered networks. If such link-state information is delayed it can be difficult for those applications to adequately fulfill their intended functionality. This document describes extensions to ISIS supporting distribution of fragment origination time. The origination time can be used to aid troubleshooting and/or by the applications themselves to improve their behavior. Timestamping can be also used to detect replay attack which are not addressed in IS-IS currently. Additionally, a mechanism is proposed by which the consistency of databases on all routers in the network can be easily verified and a rough metric of diffusion behavior derived.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: Many applications in today’s networks rely on safe, reliable and timely flooding of link-state information, such as, but not limited to Traffic Engineered networks and advanced telemetry solutions. If such information is delayed during flooding it can be difficult for those applications to adequately fulfill their intended purpose. This document describes extensions to ISIS allowing it to carry the origination time on each packet. The origination time can be used to aid troubleshooting of large domains and/or by the applications themselves to improve their behavior. Further, the addition of timestamps into IS-IS packets allows to address replay attacks. Thus, IIHs can carry optional timestamps and LSPs will additionally contain in the timestamp the original lifetime used when originating the fragment in question.

As an example, in the case of Traffic Engineered Networks synchronization of the Traffic Engineering Database (TED) enables the compute nodes to adapt to changes in the network state and/or react to network events in a timely manner. If link state information is delayed during the flooding process this can result in an unsynchronized TED and easily lead to service degradation due to substandard re-optimization of network load. More specifically, in RSVP-TE networks, a TE path computed using a specific snapshot of the TED may be rejected during signaling by a transit node because of bandwidth unavailability on a specific link (link bandwidth information in the snapshot of TED used during computation may not be “current”). When the ingress is subsequently notified of this “error” via RSVP signaling, the link in question is avoided in the subsequent path computation and an alternate path is sought. An implementation may use a configurable “hold time” to determine how long this link needs to be avoided. The awareness of the distribution delay statistics can be used by implementations to dynamically adapt an appropriate “hold time” for a given TE link (instead of using a blanket topology-wide configuration). Therefore, the origination time proposed in this document is meant to be used by a compute node(s) or by an operator of Traffic Engineered Network to measure any delays incurred in TED synchronization. The awareness of delays in the distribution of information can be incorporated further into algorithms and network tooling to improve the responsiveness and quality of decisions taken.

As a second application, attackers attempting to replay previously recorded authenticated exchanges between nodes will be deflected by the timestamping mechanism refusing to accept packets failing the required sanity checks.

Ultimately, it is useful in large networks when they are in a stable state to observe whether all databases have synchronized properly and derive the delays involved in the propagation of information across the network. This document proposes an extension to the yang schema that allows easy access to such information.

section.title: Terminology
section.t: The following terms are used throughout this document:

dl.dd: A time source on a router that is derived from an external synchronization mechanism such as NTP , PTP , or a local hardware clock of sufficient quality (e.g. a stratum 0 module). A router operating with Synced Time is considered to have an authoritative clock for the purposes of this specification.

A time approximation on a router that has no Synced Time available. Proxy Time is derived from the timestamp carried in an IIH received from an adjacent neighbor that does possess Synced Time. Proxy Time is inherently less precise than Synced Time as it accumulates the precision error of the source plus any propagation delay on the link. A router operating with Proxy Time SHOULD reflect this reduced precision in the Precision field of any timestamps it originates.

A timestamp TLV in which all time-value fields (Seconds, Fraction, and Precision) are set to zero. A Zero Timestamp signals that the originating node supports the timestamping capability but does not currently possess a usable time source. A Zero Timestamp MUST NOT be used for replay protection or Proxy Time derivation. A Zero Timestamp MAY only be carried in an Adjacency Timestamp TLV on IIH packets; it MUST NOT appear in LSP Timestamp TLVs or in Adjacency Timestamp TLVs on SNP, CSNP, or ASH packets.

A timestamp carried in the Adjacency Timestamp TLV, used in IIH, SNP, CSNP, and ASH packets. It includes a nonce that binds the timestamp to the current adjacency instance. On IIH packets a Zero Timestamp is permitted to indicate capability without a time source. On SNP, CSNP, and ASH packets the timestamp MUST always be a Non-Zero Timestamp.

A timestamp carried in the LSP Timestamp TLV, used exclusively in LSP fragments. It indicates the point in time the fragment with its current sequence number was generated and optionally carries the originating lifetime. An LSP Timestamp MUST always be a Non-Zero Timestamp; a node without a usable time source MUST NOT include an LSP Timestamp TLV.

A timestamp TLV carrying a time value in which at least the Seconds or Fraction field is non-zero. A Non-Zero Timestamp represents an actual point in time and may convey either Synced Time (P-Bit = 0) or Proxy Time (P-Bit = 1).
A Non-Zero Timestamp that passes the applicable acceptance rules defined in this document. Only a Valid Non-Zero Timestamp may be used for replay protection decisions or Proxy Time derivation.

A Non-Zero Timestamp that fails the applicable acceptance rules. A packet bearing an Invalid Non-Zero Timestamp is subject to the rejection or hold-down procedures specified in the relevant acceptance section.

section.title: Timestamp TLVs
section.t: This section defines two new, optional TLVs for carrying timestamps in ISIS packets. The two TLVs are distinguished by type code: the Adjacency Timestamp TLV is used in IIH, SNP, CSNP, and ASH packets and carries an adjacency nonce, while the LSP Timestamp TLV is used exclusively in LSP fragments and carries the originating lifetime. In case of multiple instances of a timestamp TLV in a packet only the first occurrence MUST be used. The absence of a timestamp TLV signifies that such information is not available due to a host of possible issues, one of them lack of clock with synchronization precise enough.

Both TLVs share a common time encoding. To save space the timestamp follows semantically the NTP seconds epoch with the exception of an extra bit in the seconds field to extend the wrap around and carrying approximately 1 millisecond resolution in the fractional part of the timestamp since this is considered sufficient for link-state purposes. The specification follows further guidelines of as far as possible.

section.title: Adjacency Timestamp TLV
section.t: When present in an IIH, SNP, CSNP, or ASH packet, this TLV carries the origination time and a locally generated nonce that binds the timestamp to the current adjacency instance.

ul.li: Type: TBD1
Length: 10 (fixed).
Seconds: 4 bytes of number of seconds since the NTP epoch.

H(-Bit): 1 bit. Extra high order bit is used to prevent wrap-around in 2036 and pushes it out to 2242. The offset can be constructed in network order as 33rd bit of a 64 bits value and the `Seconds` field OR'ed into the lower order bits of the according value.
P(-Bit): 1 bit. Proxy Time indicator. When set to 0, the originator is using Synced Time (as defined in ). When set to 1, the originator is using Proxy Time derived from a neighbor's IIH timestamp.

Fraction: 10 bits representing the fractional part of the second in units of 2^-10 which is equivalent to approximately 1 millisecond resolution. The value MUST be less than 1024. Any value greater than 1024 MUST be treated as 1024 milliseconds.

Precision: 4 bits indicating the maximum possible slip (either in future or past) of the time source used to generate the timestamp as 2^Precision milliseconds. The time source may be a synchronization protocol (such as NTP or PTP), a local hardware clock (such as a stratum 0 receiver), or an internal oscillator. The advertised value MUST reflect the worst-case accuracy achievable by whatever mechanism provides the time. This yields a range from 1 millisecond (value 0) to 32768 milliseconds (value 15). Values resulting in precision worse than 1024 milliseconds MUST be treated as indicating 1024 milliseconds by the receiver. A node that cannot achieve a precision of 1024 milliseconds or better MUST advertise a Zero Timestamp (as defined in ) to indicate capability without a usable time source.

Nonce: 4 bytes. A locally generated random value chosen when the adjacency transitions from DOWN to INIT. The nonce MUST remain constant for the lifetime of the adjacency instance. A new random nonce MUST be generated each time the adjacency enters INIT state.

section.t: A Zero Timestamp (all time fields zero) still carries the nonce. This signals timestamping capability and binds the adjacency instance even when no usable time source is available. A Zero Timestamp MAY only appear in an Adjacency Timestamp TLV carried on IIH packets. On SNP, CSNP, and ASH packets the Adjacency Timestamp TLV MUST carry a Non-Zero Timestamp; a node without a usable time source MUST NOT include the Adjacency Timestamp TLV on those packet types.

section.title: LSP Timestamp TLV
section.t: When contained in a fragment this TLV indicates the point in time the fragment with the current sequence number has been generated and carries the original lifetime used. A node without a usable time source MUST NOT include this TLV.

For practical purposes, although desirable, timestamping the moment a fragment is flooded would be preferable but beside practical implementation problems this could generate on different interfaces the same fragment with different content which breaks one of the fundamental tenants of link-state protocols. However, an implementation is free to choose to use, e.g. the moment the fragment is queued for flooding first time rather than the time the version is generated.

ul.li: Type: TBD2

Length: Indicates the length of content and allows to deduce whether the originating lifetime is contained in it or not. A length of 6 contains only the timestamp while a length of 8 indicates that originating lifetime is included.
Seconds: 4 bytes of number of seconds since the NTP epoch.

H(-Bit): 1 bit. Extra high order bit is used to prevent wrap-around in 2036 and pushes it out to 2242. The offset can be constructed in network order as 33rd bit of a 64 bits value and the `Seconds` field OR'ed into the lower order bits of the according value.
P(-Bit): 1 bit. Proxy Time indicator. When set to 0, the originator is using Synced Time (as defined in ). When set to 1, the originator is using Proxy Time derived from a neighbor's IIH timestamp.

Fraction: 10 bits representing the fractional part of the second in units of 2^-10 which is equivalent to approximately 1 millisecond resolution. The value MUST be less than 1024. Any value greater than 1024 MUST be treated as 1024 milliseconds.

Precision: 4 bits indicating the maximum possible slip (either in future or past) of the time source used to generate the timestamp as 2^Precision milliseconds. The advertised value MUST reflect the worst-case accuracy achievable by whatever mechanism provides the time. This yields a range from 1 millisecond (value 0) to 32768 milliseconds (value 15). Values resulting in precision worse than 1024 milliseconds MUST be treated as indicating 1024 milliseconds by the receiver. A node that cannot achieve a precision of 1024 milliseconds or better MUST NOT include an LSP Timestamp TLV.
Originating Lifetime: Indicates the value of the LSP remaining lifetime field when the LSP was originated (Length = 8). If the originating lifetime is not available, the TLV is sent with Length = 6.

section.title: Replay Attack Protection
section.t: The timestamp field MUST NOT be used if the packet is not authenticated by cryptographic signature or hash. Further considerations are outlined in .

To begin the discussion in this chapter the interval of (indicated precision in the packet + local precision) multiplied by a small constant is denoted by small delta or |S.
Since some things like LSP lifetime has a relatively coarse time resolution, the interval of (indicated precision in the packet + local precision) multiplied by a larger constant is used and denoted by large delta or |L. For practical purposes |L is likely to span several seconds.

When a received packet has the P-Bit set (indicating Proxy Time as defined in ), a constant not smaller than 1 second MUST be added to the indicated precision before computing |S or |L. This additional allowance is denoted as |P and accounts for the inherent inaccuracy of a clock derived from a neighbor's timestamp rather than a direct synchronization source.
When timestamped, packets can be protected against replay attacks by following acceptance rules.

section.title: IIH Nonce Considerations
section.t: A Zero Timestamp carries no time value and therefore cannot be validated against a local clock. Without an additional mechanism, an attacker that captures a Zero Timestamp IIH (for example during adjacency formation when the neighbor has not yet acquired a time source) could replay it at any later point to disrupt an established adjacency. The nonce field in the Adjacency Timestamp TLV exists to bind each IIH to a specific adjacency instance, closing this replay vector without requiring time-based validation of every packet.

The nonce is generated locally by each node when entering INIT state and remains constant for the lifetime of that adjacency instance. The receiver records the neighbor's nonce at the moment the adjacency reaches UP (3-way handshake complete). While the adjacency is UP, any IIH carrying a mismatched nonce is suspect. However, a blanket rejection of mismatched nonces would prevent fast recovery after a neighbor reboot: the rebooted node generates a fresh nonce and its IIHs would be dropped until the hold timer expires.

The solution is to accept a new nonce if and only if the IIH also carries a Valid Non-Zero Timestamp. A valid timestamp proves that the packet was generated recently (within |S of the local clock) and is therefore not a replay of a pre-existing capture. This allows immediate adjacency continuity after a reboot where the node already possesses a synchronized clock. Conversely, a rebooted node that has no clock yet (and therefore sends a Zero Timestamp with its new nonce) cannot prove freshness and must wait for the neighbor's hold timer to expire — the only case where the standard IS-IS timeout-based recovery applies.

section.title: IIH Acceptance Rules
section.t: A node MUST track per adjacency the neighbor's nonce as received in the Adjacency Timestamp TLV. The nonce is recorded when the adjacency first reaches the UP state (3-way handshake complete). Additionally, the node tracks whether a Non-Zero Timestamp (as defined in ) has been observed from the neighbor (the "valid-timestamp-seen" flag).
The following rules govern acceptance of IIH packets with respect to timestamping:

ul.li: While the adjacency is in DOWN or INIT state, an IIH with or without the Adjacency Timestamp TLV is accepted (subject to normal IS-IS authentication). No nonce or timestamp validation is performed below 3-way.

When the adjacency transitions to UP, the nonce from the neighbor's Adjacency Timestamp TLV is recorded as the "active nonce" for this adjacency. If no Adjacency Timestamp TLV was present in the IIH that completed the 3-way handshake, no nonce is recorded and timestamp-based protection is not active for this adjacency.
While the adjacency is UP and an active nonce is recorded, an IIH received without the Adjacency Timestamp TLV MUST be silently dropped.

While the adjacency is UP and an active nonce is recorded, an IIH carrying a Valid Non-Zero Timestamp with a nonce differing from the active nonce MUST be accepted. The active nonce MUST be updated to the new value. This covers the case of a neighbor that has rebooted and generated a fresh nonce but already possesses a valid time source. The Valid Non-Zero Timestamp proves the packet is not a replay.

While the adjacency is UP and an active nonce is recorded, an IIH carrying a Zero Timestamp or an Invalid Non-Zero Timestamp with a nonce differing from the active nonce MUST be silently dropped. Without a Valid Non-Zero Timestamp to prove freshness, a nonce mismatch is indistinguishable from a replay.

While the adjacency is UP and an active nonce is recorded, an IIH carrying an Invalid Non-Zero Timestamp (i.e. deviating more than |S from the local clock, accounting for |P if the P-Bit is set) with the correct nonce SHOULD be dropped.

While the adjacency is UP, the valid-timestamp-seen flag is set, and the active nonce matches, an IIH carrying a Zero Timestamp SHOULD be dropped. A neighbor that has previously demonstrated a functioning time source is not expected to revert to no clock without the adjacency transitioning through DOWN first.

While the adjacency is UP and the valid-timestamp-seen flag is NOT set, an IIH carrying a Zero Timestamp with the correct nonce MUST be accepted but MUST NOT be used for replay checking or Proxy Time derivation.

section.title: Fast Adjacency Reset
section.t: A node that wishes to signal an intentional adjacency reset to its neighbor MAY send an IIH in INIT state carrying the Adjacency Timestamp TLV with the currently active nonce. Because the nonce matches, the receiver can distinguish this from a replayed packet and immediately transition the adjacency to DOWN without waiting for the hold timer to expire.

section.title: LSP Acceptance Rules
section.t: When timestamped, LSPs packets that trigger any of the criteria

ul.li: (originating timestamp + originating lifetime) is smaller than ( current local time - |L )
LSP lifetime larger than originating lifetime
(originating timestamp + LSP lifetime) deviating more than |L from current local time
originating timestamp smaller than the last accepted timestamp for this fragment (except purges)

section.t: SHOULD not be accepted.

The last condition allows specifically for sending packets with the same timestamp within a small window of time. Attempts to tighten this further would limit the maximum rates of packet issuance given the timestamp resolution and impose further very strict packet queuing limitations. An attempted replay attack within this window is detectable by arrival of excessive amount of identical IIH or SNP packets within a small window of time and should be tracked and reported.
Packets arriving on the wire SHOULD undergo timestamp sanity checking as soon as possible after being cryptographically authenticated.

Purging presents a particularly difficult problem since mandates the acceptable TLVs in a purge and timestamping is currently not part of those TLVs. Due to this precondition, a change in standard is needed and timestamping on purging can only be originated after upgrade of the whole domain. Additionally, purges carry a lifetime of 0 which defeats the timestamp criteria as defined above and thus need a different set of rules. Purges that trigger any of the criteria

ul.li: timeststamp contains originating lifetime different from 0.
(originating timestamp + |L) is the future compared to current local time
originating timestamp less or equal to the timestamp seen on the last purge for this LSP
originating timestamp smaller than the last accepted timestamp for this fragment

section.t: SHOULD be discarded.

section.title: Proxy Time Derivation
section.t: A node that has not yet synchronized a precise internal clock (e.g. has not acquired NTP synchronization) SHOULD derive its Proxy Time from the average of the timestamps received in IIH packets from its adjacent neighbors. This averaging reduces the impact of any single neighbor having a slightly skewed clock.

When computing this average, a node MUST ignore IIH timestamps that have the P-Bit set. Only timestamps originating from neighbors with Synced Time (P=0) are eligible as input for Proxy Time derivation. This prevents compounding of inaccuracies through successive diffusion of proxy-derived clocks across multiple hops.
A node operating with Proxy Time MUST set the P-Bit on all timestamps it originates (in IIHs, SNPs and LSPs).

section.title: Operational and Deployment Considerations
section.t: A requirement for the correct interpretation of the additions proposed in this document is an infrastructure capable of synchronizing time across devices involved so the timestamps at the various points of interest become comparable. This could be accomplished by utilizing NTP , Precision Time Protocol (PTP) IEEE Std. 1588 or 802.1AS designed for bridged LANs. The achieved precision is carried in the timestamp of the fragment.

Though the timestamp can be very useful in deriving measurement of behavior in a deployed IS-IS network, e.g. maximum incurred flooding delays between any pair of nodes, it should not be used in any attempts to modify the behavior of protocol behavior itself such as e.g. influencing flooding rates. A single badly synchronized clock could otherwise change the behavior of parts or even the whole network in unpredictable or even detrimental way. Replay protection as defined in is an exception.

section.title: Security Considerations
section.t: For practical reasons, the timestamping replay protection defined in this document relies on different mechanisms than negotiation and repetition of nonces. It preconditions clock synchronization across nodes and hence presents an attack vector where the necessary clock mechanisms can be compromised if vulnerable. The attack windows and vectors are otherwise comparable due to the nature of IGPs which do not rely on lossless communication channels.

The replay protection mechanisms for IIH packets defined in this document rely on the IS-IS three-way handshake as defined in to prevent an attacker from exploiting adjacency state transitions to reset timestamp tracking state. Accordingly, IS-IS three-way handshake MUST be deployed on all interfaces and cryptographic authentication MUST be enabled before IIH timestamping is used for replay attack protection. If either precondition is not met, IIH timestamps MUST NOT be relied upon for replay protection and SHOULD be used for informational purposes only. LSP replay protection as defined in this document does not depend on the three-way handshake but MUST only be employed when cryptographic authentication of LSPs is enabled.

section.title: Yang Extensions for Database Fingerprint
section.t: To allow for quick validation of database synchronization across all nodes a node can implement yang extensions providing the checksum of all fragments per level. The extension includes the time difference from the last fingerprint change which facilitates measurement of flooding behavior across the network.
Aged out LSPs are excluded from the fingerprint calculation.
Reference checksum algorithm for a fragment is given in . The overall fingerprint is the XOR of all fragment checksums.

    pub(crate) fn lsdb_fingerprint_component(&self) -> u64 {
        let mut result: u64 = 0;
        let system_id: &[u8] = self.lsp_id.system_id.as_ref();
        for i in system_id.iter().chain(&[self.lsp_id.pseudonode]) {
            result <<= 8;
            result ^= *i as u64;
        }
        // fragment checksum
        result ^= (self.cksum as u64) << 48;
        // This is equal to the PDU length advertised by the fragment
        result ^= (self.raw.len() as u64) << 32;
        result
    }
